claims.text: A critical valence electron concentration threshold governs the relative stability of FCC and BCC phases in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Crossing the critical VEC threshold shifts the free-energy landscape.
Crossing the critical VEC threshold induces an abrupt change in FCC and BCC phase fractions.
The threshold-induced phase change optimizes the balance among high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
The proposed baseline alloy has a VEC near the expected critical threshold.
Controlled changes in Al content, potentially supplemented by minor Co or Cr substitutions, can systematically vary VEC.
FCC and BCC phase fractions and their spatial distributions are modulated by VEC.
Changing VEC modifies the alloy's electronic structure.
Changing VEC modifies the free-energy balance between competing FCC and BCC structures.
At the critical VEC, an inflection in the free-energy curve triggers an abrupt transition in whether FCC or BCC predominates.
The transition produces a duplex FCC/BCC phase architecture.
A duplex FCC/BCC architecture provides an optimal combination of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
Compositions straddling the critical VEC will exhibit a marked shift in their FCC:BCC phase fractions relative to the baseline.
The predicted phase change will be observable through diffraction and microstructural imaging.
Mechanical and environmental performance will improve near the optimum VEC.
The hypothesis is applicable to cast and homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs under near-equilibrium conditions.
The hypothesis may not extend to non-equilibrium processing or substantially different compositional schemes because other effects may dominate.
Theoretical and empirical literature supports an influence of VEC on phase stability in HEAs.
Compositional and processing changes confound attempts to isolate VEC as the governing variable.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described simultaneously as equilibrium, as-cast, and homogenized. An as-cast state and an as-homogenized state are distinct processing states, so the intended baseline state is internally ambiguous.
